paras: The lynching of Avery Mills took place on August 28, 1900, near Forest City in Rutherford County, North Carolina, when armed men took Mills, a young Black tenant farmer, from two officers carrying him to jail and shot him to death. Mills had been arrested that morning, accused of killing his white landlord, Mills H. Flack, a former state legislator. Accounts presented the killing as the fulfillment of Flack's dying wish, and the wire brief added that a mob went looking for Mills's wife.

Mills was working a crop on Flack's plantation, and some days earlier his wife had ordered Flack off the place, the second time with a pistol, when he came for fruit. The Associated Press brief, reprinted in the Richmond Planet, said instead that the trouble arose over a theft of peaches by Mills.

About 9 a.m. on August 28, Flack and his son Otho came to the farm to pull fodder, and Mills stopped them and renewed the argument. In the Charlotte dispatch, Mills shot Flack with a pistol his wife brought, and was himself wounded by Flack's shotgun and by the son, who shot him in the hip. The Raleigh News and Observer's correspondent wrote that Flack fired first, "it is thought, to frighten the negro," and the Atlanta Constitution reported that Mills said Flack's party had threatened to shoot his wife. Flack died within an hour, after saying he wanted Mills hanged and wanted his friends to see it done.

Justice J. C. Green committed Mills and his wife to jail, and Town Marshal Hamrick and Constable Hardin set out with them by wagon for Rutherfordton. Armed men on horseback and in vehicles overtook the wagon two and a half miles from Forest City, while Sheriff Martin held back a second crowd a few hundred yards away. Town Marshal J. D. Justice of Rutherfordton, O. C. Erwin, and Hardin pleaded with the men, and Hamrick drew his revolver and tried to drive on, but Mills was pulled from the wagon. As the sheriff approached, the men threw Mills against the bank of the road and shot him, and he died in less than a minute. The Charlotte Observer's correspondent put the shooters at no more than a dozen; the News and Observer described a mob of about 100.

Mills's wife was jailed as an accessory, and the wire brief reported that a mob had gone in search of her; the coverage does not show what became of her. Rutherfordton informants said the mob worked "in the most orderly manner" and dispersed quietly, and no report of an inquest or arrests appears in the coverage.

The fullest white version, a Charlotte dispatch, ran in the Washington Times under "RIDDLED WITH BULLETS" and ended "His dying wish was carried out to the letter." An eyewitness letter from the Charlotte Observer's Rutherfordton correspondent ran in the Norfolk Virginian-Pilot and the Burke County News. A short Associated Press brief naming only "a white man named Flack" ran from Savannah and Indianapolis to small weeklies in Kentucky, Pennsylvania, and Virginia into September.

Headlines took Flack's side: the Delaware Gazette wrote "Death of a Prominent North Carolinian Soon Avenged" and called Mills reputedly "a desperate character," and the Atlanta Constitution wrote "PLANTER'S DEATH AVENGED." In the Watauga Democrat the victim became "An unknown negro."

The only Black-press item found, in the Richmond Planet of September 1, was the wire brief under "COLORED MAN LYNCHED," with "colored" in place of "negro" and Flack spelled "Flask." It ran without comment among local notices.

Most reports said Mills was shot, but the Delaware Gazette said the mob first "swung him to a tree" and then riddled his body. The landlord appears as Mills H., Miles H., and W. H. Flack, and the Yorkville Enquirer said Mills fired a shotgun rather than a pistol.

reader.title: Lynching of Avery Mills
bases: A crowd took Mills from Town Marshal Hamrick and Constable Hardin on the way to jail and shot him dead (A1, A20, A21).
Mills was taken from officers and shot dead by a crowd of at least a dozen (A21, A19, A5) acting, by the papers' account, to avenge Flack and carry out his wish that Mills be hanged (A1, A2).

The Charlotte dispatch (A1), the Raleigh News and Observer's special (A5), an eyewitness Rutherfordton letter (A20, A21), and the Atlanta Constitution's Rutherfordton special (A19) agree that Mills was taken from officers and shot.

accounts.label: Charlotte dispatch
accounts.gist: Mills, in a fruit dispute with his landlord, shot Flack with a pistol his wife brought; a crowd took him from officers and shot him in a volley at noon.

accounts.label: Rutherfordton correspondent (eyewitness)
accounts.gist: The reporter warned the officers of armed pursuers; despite pleas, a crowd pulled Mills from the wagon and no more than a dozen men shot him against the road bank as the sheriff approached.

accounts.label: News and Observer special
accounts.gist: Flack fired his shotgun first, apparently to frighten Mills, who then shot him; a mob of about 100 emptied buckshot into Mills and dispersed in orderly fashion.

accounts.label: Mills's claim, as reported
accounts.gist: Mills said Flack's party had threatened to shoot his wife over fruit taken from the orchard.

accounts.label: Delaware version
accounts.gist: Flack accused Mills of stealing peaches; the mob hanged Mills to a tree and then shot the body.

accounts.label: Associated Press brief
accounts.gist: An unnamed negro was lynched for the murder of a white man named Flack over stolen peaches; a mob went in search of the woman who brought the gun.

framing.detail: Washington Times: 'Negro Slain by a Mob for Killing a White Man' ending 'His dying wish was carried out to the letter.'
Delaware Gazette: 'Death of a Prominent North Carolinian Soon Avenged', Mills 'a desperate character'; Atlanta Constitution: 'PLANTER'S DEATH AVENGED'.
News and Observer 'TENANT KILLS LANDLORD' reports Flack may have fired first but stresses the mob's orderliness.
The eyewitness Rutherfordton letter details officers' and citizens' pleas to let the law take its course.
The AP brief ran unnamed and unchanged in many papers.
Richmond Planet: 'COLORED MAN LYNCHED', the AP brief with 'colored' for 'negro', no comment.

Avery Mills killed; his unnamed wife jailed and threatened with lynching.

info: Tuesday, August 28, 1900; Flack shot about 9 a.m., Mills killed about noon (11 o'clock or afternoon in other reports)
On the road from Forest City toward the Rutherfordton jail, two and a half miles from Forest City at the old Eaves place; Mills taken about 100 yards from the road
Avery Mills, Black, about 21, tenant/renter on Flack's plantation; his wife (unnamed) jailed and threatened with lynching
Accused of shooting and killing Mills H. Flack, his white landlord and a former state legislator; wife accused as accessory for bringing the gun
Armed white men from the Forest City area, on horseback and in vehicles; not identified; no disguises
